newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Afghan instability casts shadow over Tajik peace deal.
newsitem.headline: Afghan instability casts shadow over Tajik peace deal.

text.p: Clashes on Tajikistan's border with Afghanistan this week have underscored fears that the Afghan conflict could threaten a peace accord aimed at ending a four-year civil war in the ex-Soviet state.
On Tuesday, Russian border guards reported a clash with Tajik opposition guerrillas along the Tajik-Afghan frontier which they said left 30 guerrillas dead.
The Tajik opposition have denied any involvement in the clash but the incident comes unnervingly close to a Tajik peace deal due to be signed on June 27.

"We consider this incident a provocation by some circles in the Russian military," said Akbar Turajonzoda, hardline deputy leader of the Tajik opposition. "They want to undermine the process of a peaceful settlement in Tajikistan," he said.
Tajikistan, a remote Central Asian state thrown across the rugged Tien Shan and Pamir mountain ranges, fell apart in a civil war in 1992, killing many thousands.

Islamist opposition guerrillas fighting Tajikistan's secular government operated out of camps in northern Afghanistan, with part of the opposition leadership based in the northern Afghan town of Taloqan.

Around 20,000 Russian troops guard the republic's borders with Afghanistan and China and have performed some peacekeeping duties. Russia sees keeping fundamentalist Islam out of its former Central Asian colonies as a vital strategic interest.
"Russia is not only a European state but an Asian one as well," the commander of Russia's border forces, General Andrei Nikolayev, said earlier this year of his troops' presence in Tajikistan.

Drug trafficking has also created instability along Tajikistan's leaky borders with Afghanistan and is now a major transit point for Afghan opium on its way to western Europe, with profits from the trade helping to finance both wars.
Links in the Tajik and Afghan wars began to flow the other way last year following the fall of the Afghan capital Kabul to the purist Islamic Taleban militia last September.
The commander of ousted Afghan government forces, Ahmad Shah Masood, is supplied partly by helicopters flying out of an airbase in Tajikistan's southern town of Kulyab.
Masood is also an ethnic Tajik, underlining Central Asia's strong cross-border ethnic ties with Afghanistan, home also to Uzbeks and Turkmens.
Tajik opposition fighters, with their flat pancake hats, straggly beards and training in Afghanistan are hard to distinguish from Afghan mujahedin.
"There is obviously a connection between the two conflicts," said a western diplomat based in the Tajik capital Dushanbe.

"Tajikistan and Russian troops there were very nervous about Taleban advances northwards and what effect that might have but Taleban setbacks in the last couple of weeks have tempered that a bit," he said.

Diplomats and aid workers in Tajikistan said last month's push north by the Taleban to try and win complete control of Afghanistan threatened the arrival of refugees and retreating Afghan fighters on Tajik territory.
The presence of armed mujahedin Tajikistan, itself a complicated patchwork of independent fiefdoms and armed bands, could further destabilise the republic, they say.
A ceasefire in Tajikistan has held since December.
But Tuesday's clash and a reported build up of Tajik and government forces near the Tajik capital Dushanbe have heightened tensions before the June 27 signing.
"Everyone is very concerned (by clashes) as the 27th is coming up fast," the diplomat said.
